title: Gulberg Townhouse

gallery.caption: Living room — oak veneer panelling, plaster ceiling coves, layered 2700K lighting
Kitchen — book-matched walnut island with a solid-surface waterfall edge
Primary bedroom — upholstered headboard wall and blackout-integrated curtains
Stair — blackened steel stringers with a hand-finished timber rail
Joinery detail — 1.5 mm tolerance on a 4.2 m wardrobe run

excerpt: A 1970s townhouse re-planned around daylight, a single walnut palette and storage that disappears into the walls.
summary: The house had good bones and thirty years of accumulated partitions. We removed four walls, moved the stair, and rebuilt the ground floor as one continuous sequence of living spaces that all borrow light from the rear garden.
challenge: Three generations under one roof, a structural wall where the client wanted an opening, and a brief that asked for calm without asking for minimal.
approach: We ran a structural survey in week one, proposed a steel beam that freed the ground floor, and developed a single material family — oak, walnut, lime plaster and unlacquered brass — repeated at three scales so the house reads as one idea rather than eleven rooms.
result: Nineteen weeks from demolition to styling. The family moved in over a weekend, the snag list closed in nine days, and the kitchen island has since become the family's default gathering point.

specs.v: Engineered oak 190 mm plank, honed terrazzo wet areas

testimonial.quote: They told us the truth about the structural wall in the first meeting, which is why we trusted everything after it.
testimonial.name: Family client

title: MM Alam Flagship

gallery.caption: Ground floor — fluted plaster walls, brass rails, 3000K merchandise lighting at 900 lux
First floor — fitting suite with a seated waiting bay and full-length mirror wall
Ceiling detail — recessed track with a 12° optic over mannequin plinths

excerpt: A two-floor flagship designed as a rollout prototype: every fixture documented so store two costs less than store one.
summary: The brand needed a flagship that could also function as a manual. We designed the store, built it in nine weeks, then wrote a 74-page rollout pack covering fixtures, tolerances, lighting and approved substitutions.
challenge: A trading date fixed by the landlord, a narrow 7.2 m frontage, and a brand book written for European store sizes.
approach: We compressed the journey into three zones — decompression, discovery, decision — and designed fixtures in modular 900 mm bays so the same kit works in a 1,200 sq ft mall unit and a 6,000 sq ft flagship.
result: Opened on the committed date. The rollout pack has since been used for four further stores in three cities, with an 18% reduction in fit-out cost per square foot.

specs.v: 4 stores delivered from the same pack

testimonial.quote: The rollout manual paid for the flagship. Our fourth store came in eighteen percent cheaper per square foot.
testimonial.name: Head of Retail

title: Systems Ltd HQ

gallery.caption: Open floor — 184 bench desks with acoustic screens and a 45 dB target
Reception — terrazzo counter, backlit brand wall and a planted arrival court
Focus rooms — linear 4000K task light with individual occupancy control

excerpt: Two floors, 184 desks, eleven meeting rooms and a café — delivered on one contract with the business still trading below.
summary: Systems Ltd outgrew three separate floors in two buildings. We consolidated them into a single 24,600 sq ft head office designed around six team adjacencies and a shared café spine.
challenge: The company could not stop operating, the building management restricted noisy works to evenings, and the existing HVAC could not cope with the new density.
approach: A phased programme in three zones, MEP redesign with added fresh-air capacity, and a night-shift joinery install so the floor was usable every Monday morning. Furniture was factory-inspected twice before delivery.
result: Handed over two days ahead of programme with a 22-item snag list, all closed within eleven days. Post-occupancy measurement recorded 43 dB on the open floor against a 45 dB target.

specs.v: 43 dB open floor, NRC 0.85 ceiling rafts

testimonial.quote: One contract, one number to call. Our facilities manager described it as the first fit-out she did not have to manage.
testimonial.name: Director of Operations

title: Qissa Coffee House

gallery.caption: Counter — cast terrazzo front, walnut back bar and a 3-metre espresso run
Material study — terrazzo, walnut, lime plaster, unlacquered brass
Evening room — 2400K table light with absorbent ceiling rafts

excerpt: A 1,450 sq ft café built around a three-metre counter, a queue line that never blocks the door, and acoustics that survive a full house.
summary: Qissa wanted a neighbourhood café with the throughput of a city store. The design starts at the espresso machine and works outwards to seating, queue and street.
challenge: A 1,450 sq ft shell with a single service riser, a 60-cover ambition, and a neighbouring residential floor that objects to noise after 11pm.
approach: We modelled the queue at 42 covers per hour, moved the pastry case to break the line, specified absorbent ceiling rafts and a 2400K evening scene, and routed extraction through a silencer box on the rear elevation.
result: Seven weeks from site start to first pour. Average dwell time settled at 47 minutes with turnover maintained at 38 covers per hour through the morning peak.

specs.v: 3.0 m cast terrazzo, walnut back bar
NRC rafts, 74 dB at full house

testimonial.quote: They designed the queue before they designed the ceiling. That is why our morning peak never spills onto the pavement.
testimonial.name: Founder

title: Raavi Farmhouse

gallery.caption: Main hall — double-height volume with a lime-plaster feature wall
Family room — deep seating, wool rugs and a timber batten screen to the terrace
Joinery — solid ash doors with concealed magnetic catches

excerpt: A weekend house where every room is designed for the view it borrows, and every material was chosen to age outdoors as well as in.
summary: Nine thousand eight hundred square feet arranged around a central courtyard. We coordinated with the architect on openings, then designed interiors that keep the landscape in frame from every seat.
challenge: A weekend house used hard for two days a week and closed for five — materials had to tolerate heat, dust and long idle periods without degrading.
approach: Solid timber and lime plaster instead of veneer-over-MDF in exposed locations, stone floors throughout the ground level, sealed joinery with stainless hardware, and a maintenance schedule handed over with the keys.
result: Delivered in 24 weeks including the landscape interface. Two years on, the maintenance log shows zero finish failures and one hardware adjustment.

specs.v: Solid ash, lime plaster, honed limestone

testimonial.quote: The material schedule they gave us at handover is the reason the house still looks new.
testimonial.name: Private client

title: Liberty Boutique

gallery.caption: Sales floor — eight display cases with 4000K high-CRI optics
Material palette — brushed brass, black granite, deep green lacquer

excerpt: 820 square feet, eight cases, and lighting specified to make gold read as gold under a shop ceiling.
summary: A tight Liberty Market plot re-fitted for a fourth-generation jeweller. Security, service and lighting were designed together because in a boutique they occupy the same 40 mm.
challenge: Existing structure could not be altered, trading had to continue next door, and the client wanted the display to feel precious without feeling cold.
approach: Bespoke brass-framed cases with laminated security glass, 4000K CRI-95 optics tuned for yellow metal, deep green lacquer panelling to raise contrast, and a single till position with a clear sightline to the door.
result: Six weeks including a three-night changeover. Average transaction time fell and the client has since commissioned two further counters.

testimonial.quote: The lighting alone changed how our gold looks. Customers notice before we say anything.
testimonial.name: Fourth-generation owner

title: Karandaaz Workplace

gallery.caption: Arrival lounge — community table, phone booths and a planted screen
Hot-desk floor — 96 positions across four acoustic zones
Booth detail — felt-lined interior with 4000K reading light

excerpt: A co-working floor zoned by noise level rather than by department — quiet at the core, loud at the edge.
summary: Ninety-six hot desks, fourteen private offices, six booths and a community lounge, organised as concentric acoustic zones from the street inwards.
challenge: One open floor with a single noisy street elevation, and a business model that sells silence as a product.
approach: We mapped noise sources, placed lounges and phone calls at the perimeter, and pushed deep-work desks to the quiet core behind felt-lined partitions and absorbent ceiling rafts.
result: Occupancy reached 84% within the first quarter. Post-occupancy surveys recorded a 4.6/5 rating for acoustic comfort.

testimonial.quote: Selling silence is our product. They designed the floor so the promise holds at 4pm on a Tuesday.
testimonial.name: Community Director

title: Serai Dining Room

gallery.caption: Main dining — 96 covers, banquettes, plaster vaults and 2400K table light
Bar — nine stools, backlit shelving and a copper-topped counter
Palette — lime plaster, copper, terrazzo, deep indigo upholstery

excerpt: Ninety-six covers, a working pass, and a ceiling designed so the room stays at conversation volume when it is full.
summary: A casual-dining room where the kitchen line and the dining floor were designed in the same model — because the pass, the dishwasher run and the guest entrance all compete for the same twelve metres.
challenge: A 96-cover ambition on a 4,600 sq ft shell with a fixed kitchen position, and neighbours two floors above.
approach: Plaster vaults and upholstered banquettes provide absorption without visible acoustic treatment; a copper-topped bar anchors the room; and table lighting is individually dimmed to 2400K for the evening scene.
result: Fourteen weeks including kitchen coordination. Measured 76 dB at full covers against an 78 dB target, and the room turns 2.4 times on a Friday evening.

testimonial.quote: Our chef was in the room from week one. The pass works because they designed the dining floor around it.
testimonial.name: General Manager

title: DHA Apartment Refresh

gallery.caption: Living and dining — new flooring, replanned lighting and re-faced joinery
Kitchen — replaced cabinets, quartz worktop and a new extraction route

excerpt: A nine-week renovation that kept the original terrazzo, re-faced half the joinery, and spent the budget where it changed how the flat feels.
summary: Not everything in a twenty-year-old apartment needs replacing. We kept the terrazzo and four doors, re-faced the wardrobes, and put the money into lighting, the kitchen and the two things the family complained about daily.
challenge: A live renovation with two children at home, society work-hour restrictions, and a budget that could not stretch to a full strip-out.
approach: A keep / repair / replace schedule agreed in week one, room-by-room sequencing so a bathroom and the kitchen were never both out of service, and all noisy works booked inside society hours.
result: Nine weeks, 42% below the cost of a full rebuild, and the family stayed in the apartment throughout.

testimonial.quote: They told us what not to spend money on. That conversation saved us about thirty lakh.
testimonial.name: Apartment owner

title: Indus Clinic Suite

gallery.caption: Reception and waiting — separated paediatric and adult zones
Consult corridor — six consulting rooms with acoustic doors

excerpt: Six consulting rooms, a procedure suite and two separated waiting zones — planned for hygiene routes and a calm arrival.
summary: A clinic has to satisfy two contradictory needs: efficient clinical circulation and a waiting experience that lowers a patient's heart rate. We planned both from the same model.
challenge: Strict clean/dirty separation, six consulting rooms on a narrow plate, and a brief that asked for the space not to feel clinical.
approach: Separate staff and patient circulation, acoustic doors to every consult room, warm indirect lighting and timber-look finishes in all patient-facing areas, and hard-wearing hygienic surfaces behind them.
result: Fifteen weeks to opening including equipment coordination. The clinic has since run at 92% appointment utilisation with no changes to the plan.

testimonial.quote: Patients stop asking where the paediatric side is. That was the whole point of the two-zone plan.
testimonial.name: Clinical Director
